title: Git Merge vs Rebase: What’s the Difference?

scenes.say: Ever wonder when you should merge, and when you should rebase? Let’s clear it up.
Merging keeps all the messy history and adds a merge commit. Rebasing rewrites your changes onto the latest branch, making history look clean and straight.

scenes.title: Merge vs Rebase Commands
scenes.say: When you run the merge command, you get a new merge commit. Rebasing instead takes your commits and reapplies them on top of the main branch.

scenes.label: Strategy
scenes.sub: Use rebase for local work, merge for shared branches.
scenes.say: I like to rebase my own feature branches to keep things tidy, but I use merge when bringing shared work together.

scenes.question: Should you rebase a shared branch?
scenes.wrong: Yes, always rebase for clean history.
scenes.right: No, rebasing shared branches can rewrite others’ work. Only rebase local, unshared branches.
scenes.say: Here’s a common interview trap: rebasing a branch others are using can cause big headaches. Only rebase your own local work.
